sections.heading: Asking you to stand between me and my enemies
sections.text: Lord God, you are my shelter and my defender. I cannot outfight sin, Satan, or my own weak heart, but you can. Stand with me. Hold me up when I would fall. Strengthen me when I feel unsteady. Put your protection around me so that the enemy does not have the final word. If you fight for me, I do not need to pretend I am strong on my own.
theological_themes: God is the believer’s refuge and defender in spiritual conflict.
The Christian’s strength is received from God, not produced by self-confidence.
Victory over evil depends on God’s presence and power.

scripture_references.connection: David names the Lord as rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, and stronghold. This grounds the prayer’s appeal to God as active protection rather than merely emotional comfort.

Paul teaches believers to be strong in the Lord and to stand against spiritual forces by using God’s armor. The prayer’s language of being equipped and upheld fits this dependence on God in spiritual warfare.

sections.heading: Learning to hate evil for what it really is
sections.text: Teach me to see evil without excuses. Let me hate it because it rebels against you, ruins what you made good, stains my own heart, and spreads pain wherever it goes. Do not let me make peace with anything that fights against your will. Give me a clean, serious hatred of sin—not a hatred that makes me proud, but one that makes me run back to you.
theological_themes: Sin is not harmless weakness but rebellion against God and corruption of human nature.
True repentance includes learning to see sin as God sees it.
Hatred of sin must be humble and Godward, not self-righteous.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that God’s law exposes sin as truly sinful. This supports the prayer’s request to stop minimizing evil and to see its real character before God.
The psalm calls those who love the Lord to hate evil, linking love for God with moral rejection of what opposes him. This fits the prayer’s desire for a holy, reverent opposition to sin.

sections.heading: Looking at the cross until I understand sin and mercy
sections.text: Keep bringing my eyes back to Jesus on the cross. There I see what my sin deserves, and there I see the mercy I could never earn. There is no forgiveness for me apart from your Son’s death. There is no cleansing apart from his blood. There is no answer to my guilt except the offering he made. Let the suffering of Christ show me both the ugliness of my sin and the depth of your love.
theological_themes: The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God’s mercy.
Forgiveness and cleansing come through Christ’s atoning death, not human effort.
Christ’s blood is the basis of pardon and reconciliation with God.

scripture_references.connection: Peter says Christ bore sins in his body on the tree so that believers might die to sin and live to righteousness. This directly supports the prayer’s focus on the cross as both atonement and a call to holiness.

Hebrews connects forgiveness with the shedding of blood and presents Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice as the decisive dealing with sin. This grounds the prayer’s claim that cleansing and pardon come through Christ’s death.

sections.heading: Tearing sin away instead of playing with it
sections.text: Show me the sin I keep close as the poisonous thing it is. Help me stop treating it like a harmless companion. Give me the courage to pull it away from my heart, refuse its invitations, and turn from every trap it sets. When I am tempted to negotiate with it, make me remember the cross and choose you instead.
theological_themes: Sin must be resisted decisively, not entertained or managed.
Temptation often works through hidden attachment and compromise.
The cross motivates active repentance and separation from sin.

scripture_references.connection: James calls believers to submit to God, resist the devil, and draw near to God. This fits the prayer’s movement away from sin’s snares and toward renewed nearness to the Lord.
Paul teaches that by the Spirit believers put to death the deeds of the body. The prayer’s strong language of tearing sin from the heart reflects this Spirit-enabled, active rejection of sin.

sections.heading: Clinging to Christ and living in holiness
sections.text: Lord Jesus, at your cross teach me what it would mean to be lost without you, and what you have rescued me from. Let that make me hold on to you more closely, trust you more firmly, and give myself to you more completely. Make my hatred of sin grow as my love for you grows. Let holiness become the air I breathe—the ordinary atmosphere of my life with you.
theological_themes: Christ saves from real judgment and eternal loss.
Assurance of rescue deepens faith, devotion, and gratitude.
Holiness is not an occasional act but the intended environment of the believer’s life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes final judgment as exclusion from the presence of the Lord and contrasts it with Christ being glorified in his people. This supports the prayer’s sober reflection on being saved from eternal destruction.
Paul says Christ gave himself to redeem and purify a people eager for good works. This connects the cross not only with pardon but also with a life increasingly devoted to holiness.

Peter calls believers to holiness because they were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ. This passage holds together reverent fear, redemption, and holy living in the same way this section does.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses very strong language about eternal destruction and being ‘lost.’ I preserved that sober doctrine rather than softening it, while keeping the focus on what Christ has rescued the believer from.

The original’s language of receiving ‘no wound’ could be misunderstood as a promise of immunity from all suffering or temptation. I rendered it as spiritual protection from the enemy having the final word, consistent with the prayer’s spiritual-warfare context.

The phrase ‘bruises of incarnate God’ is christologically weighty. I expressed it as the suffering of Jesus Christ, God’s Son in the flesh, without trying to explain the mystery of how the incarnate Son suffers.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the ‘foes’ primarily as sin, Satan, temptation, and the weakness of the believer’s heart, because the rest of the prayer develops the conflict as spiritual and moral rather than interpersonal.

I kept the original image of sin as poisonous by using the language of a poisonous thing kept close to the heart, preserving the force of the ‘deadly viper’ image without simply reproducing the old wording.

I rendered ‘holiness be the atmosphere in which I live’ as holiness becoming ‘the air I breathe,’ keeping the concrete image of an environment one lives in while making it natural contemporary speech.
